analysis.one_liner: Bans former members from lobbying for life and tightens revolving-door and lobbying disclosure rules.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 2010 with a single cosponsor, the bill was sent to the Senate Homeland Security Committee and died there without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made the revolving door between Congress and the lobbying business much harder to use. Former members of Congress would be barred from lobbying their old colleagues for life, instead of for two years, and senior congressional staff would face a six-year ban instead of one. Registered lobbyists would be barred for six years from taking congressional jobs with offices they had lobbied, large lobbying firms would have to publicly report which ex-lawmakers and ex-staff they hire, the penalty for false lobbying reports would rise from $200,000 to $500,000, and lobbyists would be banned from making campaign contributions.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens get a Congress whose members and senior staff are not planning their future lobbying careers while in office, plus a single searchable public website showing who is lobbying whom and which big firms employ former lawmakers. Candidates for office would no longer have their campaign committees pay for private air travel.

how_it_helps.text: Former members of Congress and elected congressional officers would face a permanent, instead of a two-year, ban on lobbying contacts with current members and staff.
Former congressional staff would face a six-year lobbying ban instead of the current one-year ban.

Registered lobbyists and foreign agents would be barred for six years from being hired by any member or committee they had substantially lobbied, with only a narrow waiver for compelling national need.
The Senate Secretary and House Clerk would have to maintain a simple, searchable public lobbying database called lobbyists.gov.

Incorporated firms with more than three registered lobbyists would have to file annual public lists of every ex-member of Congress and high-ranking ex-staff (those who made over $100,000 a year, served four years or more, or held titles like Chief of Staff or Counsel) they employ, and those filings would go to the DC U.S. Attorney for enforcement review.
The civil penalty for knowingly failing to fix a false lobbying filing would rise from $200,000 to $500,000.
Lobbyists would be banned from making campaign contributions to federal candidates, and political committees would be barred from paying for noncommercial air travel for candidates.

analysis.who_pays: Lobbying firms lose the right to hire former lawmakers and senior staff as lobbyists and face harsher disclosure and penalties. Corporations that rely on revolving-door access would find it harder to buy. Former members and senior staff could no longer turn congressional connections into lobbying income.

drawbacks.text: The bans apply to registered lobbying contacts, so the work could move to unregistered consultants and 'strategic advisors' who never file as lobbyists, shifting influence into a less visible channel rather than ending it.

A permanent ban on lobbying for ex-members, and six-year bans for staff, could discourage capable people from running for office or staying in congressional service, and could push ex-lawmakers into jobs advising lobbying firms without registering.
The six-year bar on hiring lobbyists into congressional offices includes a waiver based on 'compelling national need,' leaving an escape hatch at the discretion of the ethics committees.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a straightforward crackdown: longer cooling-off periods, more disclosure, bigger penalties, and a total ban on lobbyist campaign money. The costs are real but modest, mostly felt by lobbying firms and by former officials who would earn less selling access. The honest weakness is enforceability, since influence can migrate to unregistered consultants, but the disclosure requirements and the DC U.S. Attorney review were designed with exactly that problem in mind.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee in April 2010, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Sen. Michael Bennet introduced the Close the Revolving Door Act of 2010 on April 28, 2010, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee.
Only one senator, a Democrat, cosponsored the bill.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action of any kind; the bill died in committee when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lobbying firms and the former members and senior staff they hire came out ahead, because none of the restrictions, disclosures, or penalties ever took effect. Corporate lobbying operations kept access to ex-lawmakers and their ex-staffers intact.

for.name: Michael Bennet
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only original sponsor.

for.name: 1 of 58 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other senator joined.

against.name: Joe Lieberman
against.role: Chair, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee never held a hearing or markup on the bill or reported it out, so it never reached the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; the bill's only support came from two Democrats (the sponsor and one cosponsor), and no Republican ever signed on.

industries.note: Firms would lose the right to hire former members as lobbyists entirely and senior ex-staff for six years, and firms with more than three registered lobbyists would have to publicly name every ex-lawmaker and high-ranking ex-staffer on their payroll. They profit from the revolving door, which is exactly what the bill closes.

Companies that rely on hiring ex-members and senior ex-staff for access would face a much thinner pipeline and rougher scrutiny of their lobbying reports through the DC U.S. Attorney review. Their gain from the bill's defeat was keeping that access channel open.
Political committees would be barred from paying for noncommercial flights for candidates, shrinking a small charter market that depends on campaign funds.
